claim: KIF5A, KIF5B, and KIF5C proteins show similar developmental expression profiles in the hippocampus, with expression more prominent at early postnatal stages and significantly reduced at later postnatal and adult stages.
source: On the other hand, we found that all three KIF5 proteins showed similar developmental expression profiles in the hippocampus, with the expression more prominent at early postnatal stages and significantly reduced at later postnatal and adult stages (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing developmental expression patterns in Figure 1A

claim: All three KIF5 proteins (KIF5A, KIF5B, and KIF5C) are detected in the synaptic plasma membrane fraction.
source: All three KIF5s were detected in the synaptic plasma membrane fraction (Figure 1B), which is consistent with the proteomic study reporting the presence of three KIF5s in the PSD (Bayés et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by fractionation data in Figure 1B and cited proteomic study

claim: Knockdown of KIF5B results in a significant reduction in the frequency of miniature excitatory synaptic current (mEPSC).
source: We found that knockdown of individual KIF5 differentially affected excitatory synaptic transmission. Compared to control shRNA, knockdown of KIF5B resulted in the most profound and significant reduction in the frequency of miniature excitatory synaptic current (mEPSC), while knockdown of KIF5C did not affect mEPSC frequency or amplitude.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch recording data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Introduction of KIF5A-shRNA significantly increased the mEPSC amplitude.
source: Notably, introduction of KIF5A-shRNA did not change the mEPSC frequency but instead significantly increased the mEPSC amplitude (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 1C

claim: Knockdown of KIF5B significantly reduced the density of mushroom spines and led to a significant increase in the number of filopodia, thin and stubby spines.
source: Knockdown of KIF5B significantly reduced the density of mushroom spines and led to a significant increase in the number of filopodia, thin and stubby spines.
evidence: Supported by dendritic spine analysis data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Knockdown of KIF5C significantly decreased the number of mushroom and thin spines.
source: Knockdown of KIF5C significantly decreased the number of mushroom and thin spines (42–55 neurons of each group from three independent experiments were quantified; mean + SEM; *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001, ****p<0.0001; Kruskal-Wallis test).
evidence: Supported by dendritic spine analysis data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Knockdown of KIF5A did not cause any change in the density of mushroom spines or filopodia when compared to control neurons.
source: On the other hand, knockdown of KIF5A did not cause any change in the density of mushroom spines or filopodia when compared to control neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by dendritic spine analysis data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Co-expression of KIF5B reversed the loss of mushroom spines induced by the KIF5B-shRNA.
source: As expected, co-expression of KIF5B reversed the loss of mushroom spines induced by the KIF5B-shRNA.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Co-expression of KIF5A with the KIF5B-shRNA failed to rescue the loss of mushroom spines.
source: However, co-expression of KIF5A with the KIF5B-shRNA failed to rescue the loss of mushroom spines (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Both endogenous and exogenously expressed KIF5A and KIF5B are present in dendrites and dendritic spines.
source: Both endogenous and exogenously expressed KIF5A and KIF5B were present in dendrites and dendritic spines, and the percentage of dendritic spines containing endogenous KIF5A was even higher than that of KIF5B (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: FMRP was preferentially pulled down by KIF5B and KIF5C but not KIF5A.
source: Pull-down assay using carboxyl-terminal fragments of individual KIF5s revealed that FMRP was preferentially pulled down by KIF5B and KIF5C but not KIF5A, while all three KIF5s could pull down G3BPs and GluA2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3B

claim: All three KIF5s could pull down G3BPs and GluA2.
source: Pull-down assay using carboxyl-terminal fragments of individual KIF5s revealed that FMRP was preferentially pulled down by KIF5B and KIF5C but not KIF5A, while all three KIF5s could pull down G3BPs and GluA2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Knockdown of KIF5B significantly reduced the density of FMRP granules on dendrites.
source: Compared to control shRNA, knockdown of KIF5B significantly reduced the density of FMRP granules on dendrites.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data of GFP-FMRP granules shown in Figure 3C-D

claim: KIF5B shRNA only significantly decreased the density of stationary but not motile FMRP granules.
source: Interestingly, KIF5B shRNA only significantly decreased the density of stationary but not motile granules.
evidence: Supported by quantification of FMRP granule movement types in Figure 3D

claim: Knockdown of KIF5A caused a general increase in the density of motile FMRP granules while decreasing the stationary granules, resulting in no net change in the density of total granules.
source: In contrast, knockdown of KIF5A caused a general increase in the density of motile granules while decreasing the stationary granules, resulting in no net change in the density of total granules (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of FMRP granule movement types in Figure 3C-D

claim: Knockdown of KIF5B significantly reduced the density of both CaMKIIα and Grin2b mRNA puncta on dendrites.
source: Consistent with the reduced density of GFP-FMRP granules, knockdown of KIF5B also significantly reduced the density of both CaMKIIα and Grin2b mRNA puncta on dendrites (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Knockdown of KIF5A did not affect CaMKIIα and Grin2b mRNA density on dendrite.
source: In contrast, knockdown of KIF5A did not affect CaMKIIα and Grin2b mRNA density on dendrite.
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The last 88 amino acids of KIF5A prevent the motor protein from binding to FMRP.
source: Towards this end, we created a truncated KIF5A construct with the carboxyl-terminal lacking the last 88 amino acids, as well as a chimeric KIF5A in which the last 88 amino acids were substituted by the shorter carboxyl-terminus of KIF5B. Either one of these constructs but not the wild-type KIF5A was able to pull down FMRP from the synaptoneurosome (SNS), suggesting that the carboxyl-terminus of KIF5A indeed inhibits binding of specific cargoes (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Co-expression of the chimeric KIF5A that contained the carboxyl-terminus of KIF5B was able to reverse the spine phenotype induced by KIF5B knockdown.
source: Remarkably, when shRNA targeting KIF5B was introduced into hippocampal neurons to induce loss of mushroom spines, co-expression of the chimeric KIF5A that contained the carboxyl-terminus of KIF5B was able to reverse the spine phenotype (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4B

claim: KIF5B contains two conserved arginine residues (Arg-941 and Arg-956) followed by glycine residues (the RGG motif) that are conserved across different vertebrates.
source: Amino acid sequence alignment of the carboxyl termini of different KIF5s revealed the presence of two arginine residues (Arg-941 and Arg-956) followed by glycine residues (the RGG motif) in KIF5B that are conserved across different vertebrates.
evidence: Supported by amino acid sequence alignment shown in Figure 5A

claim: KIF5C contains only the Arg-941 but not Arg-956, while these two RGG motifs are absent in the KIF5A carboxyl-terminus.
source: KIF5C contains only the Arg-941 but not Arg-956, while these two RGG motifs are absent in the KIF5A carboxyl-terminus (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by amino acid sequence alignment shown in Figure 5A

claim: KIF5B was identified as one of the arginine-methylated proteins in the adult mouse brain by mass spectrometry.
source: Hundreds of arginine-methylated proteins in the adult mouse brain have recently been identified by mass spectrometry (Guo et al., 2014), and our data mining results indicated that KIF5B was one of the methylated proteins.
evidence: Supported by citation to mass spectrometry study (Guo et al., 2014)

claim: KIF5B and KIF5C but not KIF5A undergo arginine methylation when exogenously expressed in 293T cells.
source: We first confirmed the arginine methylation of KIF5B and KIF5C but not KIF5A when exogenously expressed in 293 T cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B

claim: KIF5B is methylated in the synaptoneurosome.
source: Using reciprocal immunoprecipitation with antibodies that recognize the mono-arginine methylation within glycine-rich region or KIF5B, we confirmed that KIF5B was methylated in the synaptoneurosome (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by reciprocal immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C

claim: R-941 and R-956 are the two major methylation sites of KIF5B.
source: The KIF5B R941H or R956H mutant showed reduced methylation, whereas arginine methylation was absent in the double mutant (R941/956H) in which both arginine residues were substituted by histidine (Figure 5D). These results indicate that R-941 and R-956 are the two major methylation sites of KIF5B.
evidence: Supported by site-directed mutagenesis and immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The amount of FMRP and G3BP1 pulled down by the methylation-deficient mutant (R941/956H) of KIF5B was significantly reduced when compared to wild-type KIF5B.
source: The amount of FMRP and G3BP1 pulled down by the methylation-deficient mutant was significantly reduced when compared to wild-type KIF5B (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Co-expression of wild-type KIF5B reversed the loss of mushroom spines induced by the knockdown of KIF5B, while the methylation-deficient KIF5B failed to rescue the mushroom spine loss.
source: Co-expression of wild-type KIF5B reversed the loss of mushroom spines induced by the knockdown of KIF5B, while the methylation-deficient KIF5B failed to rescue the mushroom spine loss (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Co-expression of wild-type but not the methylation-deficient KIF5B with the KIF5B-shRNA significantly increased the mEPSC frequency.
source: Moreover, co-expression of wild-type but not the methylation-deficient KIF5B with the KIF5B-shRNA significantly increased the mEPSC frequency, (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5G

claim: KIF5B homozygous knockout is embryonic lethal.
source: Since KIF5B homozygous knockout is embryonic lethal (Tanaka et al., 1998), we generated a KIF5B conditional knockout (Kif5b-/-) mice using the Cre/loxP gene-targeting strategy to study the function of KIF5B in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tanaka et al., 1998

claim: Both homozygous and heterozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice were viable.
source: Both homozygous and heterozygous mice were viable, and the homozygous mice did not differ in the general appearance or brain size from the wild-type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by observation and images shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Analysis of whole-brain lysate showed a significant reduction of KIF5B protein level in homozygous knockout mice when compared to wild-type.
source: Analysis of whole-brain lysate showed a significant reduction of KIF5B protein level in homozygous knockout mice when compared to wild-type, and importantly there were no significant changes in the expression of KIF5A and KIF5C (Figure 6B), or the dendritic kinesin KIF17 which is crucial for synaptic plasticity and memory formation (Song et al., 2009; Yin et al., 2011; Franker et al., 2016) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed a significant reduction of cells that were positive for both KIF5B and NRGN in the frontal association cortex (FrA) when compared to wild-type mice.
source: We found that homozygous mice showed a significant reduction of cells that were positive for both KIF5B and NRGN in the frontal association cortex (FrA) when compared to wild-type mice, without significant change in the number of neurons in this region (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Conditional knockout of KIF5B at postnatal stages resulted in a significant reduction of dendritic spines in CA1 hippocampal neurons of homozygous mice.
source: Conditional knockout of KIF5B at postnatal stages resulted in a significant reduction of dendritic spines in CA1 hippocampal neurons of homozygous mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by three-dimensional reconstruction and quantification data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The dendritic spine number was not significantly different between control and knockout mice in neurons of the frontal association cortex (FrA).
source: However, the effect of KIF5B on spine density is region-specific, since the dendritic spine number was not significantly different between control and knockout mice in neurons of the FrA (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by three-dimensional reconstruction and quantification data shown in Figure 7C

claim: CA1 hippocampal neurons of the KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed a significant reduction in both the frequency and amplitude of mEPSC as compared with wild-type neurons.
source: CA1 hippocampal neurons of the KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed a significant reduction in both the frequency and amplitude of mEPSC as compared with wild-type neurons (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch recording data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Both heterozygous and homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed a significant increase in dendritic spine elimination compared to wild-type mice over 2 days.
source: We found that both heterozygous and homozygous mice showed a significant increase in dendritic spine elimination compared to wild-type mice over 2 days (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by in vivo two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 7G

claim: Both heterozygous and homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed an increase in dendritic spine formation from Day 2 to Day 7.
source: However, when we examined the spine plasticity in the next time window from Day 2 to Day 7 over 5 days, both heterozygous and homozygous mice showed an increase in dendritic spine formation (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by in vivo two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 7H

claim: Both heterozygous and homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed an increase of dendritic spine turnover rate when compared to wild-type, but only that in homozygous was statistically significant.
source: Overall, both heterozygous and homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed an increase of dendritic spine turnover rate when compared to wild-type, but only that in homozygous was statistically significant (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by in vivo two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 7I

claim: The increase in spine formation during the second time window was caused by the significant increase in re-formation of spines in close proximity to eliminated spines from first time window.
source: Although we did not observe significant difference in the survival rate of newly formed spines (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), we found that the increase in spine formation during the second time window was caused by the significant increase in re-formation of spines in close proximity to eliminated spines from first time window (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by in vivo two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 7J

claim: There was no significant difference in open field test, elevated plus maze, and marble burying test in heterozygous and homozygous mice when compared to wild-type.
source: We found that there was no significant difference in open field test, elevated plus maze, and marble burying test in heterozygous and homozygous mice when compared to wild-type, indicating that conditional knockout of KIF5B did not lead to hyperactivity, anxiety-like or repetitive behaviors (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: Homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed a significant reduction of social memory index.
source: In 3-chamber social interaction test, homozygous mice showed a significant reduction of social memory index (Figure 8A), but no significant difference in total interaction time from wild-type (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by 3-chamber social interaction test data shown in Figure 8A

claim: Homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed a significantly reduced preference to the novel object in novel object recognition test.
source: In novel object recognition test, mice were presented with a novel object 14–16 hr after the mouse was exposed to the familiar objects for testing short-term object recognition memory. Homozygous mice showed a significantly reduced preference to the novel object (Figure 8B), suggesting a deficit in short-term memory recall.
evidence: Supported by novel object recognition test data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed a significant decrease of freezing response to the conditioned stimulus (CS, auditory cue) during the recall test 48 hr after fear acquisition.
source: The freezing response of KIF5B conditional knockout mice was similar to wild-type in the acquisition phase (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C), but homozygous mice showed a significant decrease of freezing response to the conditioned stimulus (CS, auditory cue) during the recall test 48 hr after fear acquisition (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by auditory-cued fear conditioning test data shown in Figure 8C

claim: Homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice showed a significantly higher primary latency to locate the escape hole when compared to wild-type during the recall test five days after the training in Barnes maze.
source: Homozygous mice also tended to stay in the wrong target hole instead of exploring the environment which in turn showing fewer primary errors when compared to wild-type (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D). Nonetheless, homozygous mice showed a significantly higher primary latency to locate the escape hole when compared to wild-type during the recall test five days after the training (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by Barnes maze test data shown in Figure 8D

claim: LTP could be induced in both control and homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout hippocampal slices, but the LTP decayed faster at the homozygous SC–CA1 synapses.
source: While LTP could be induced in both control and homozygous hippocampal slices, the LTP decayed faster at the homozygous SC–CA1 synapses, and the field EPSP amplitude during the last 10 min recording was significantly reduced at the homozygous SC–CA1 synapses when compared to wild-type (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by LTP recording data shown in Figure 8E

claim: There was no significant difference in input/output relationship between wild-type and homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice.
source: There was no significant difference in input/output relationship between wild-type and homozygous mice, indicating the baseline synaptic response was not affected (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by input/output curve data shown in Figure 8F

claim: There was no significant difference in pair-pulse ratio between wild-type and homozygous KIF5B conditional knockout mice.
source: To test whether presynaptic function was altered, the pair-pulse ratios were measured with several different inter-pulse durations. We found no significant difference in pair-pulse ratio between wild-type and homozygous mice, indicating similar presynaptic responses (Figure 8G).
evidence: Supported by pair-pulse ratio data shown in Figure 8G

claim: Gene duplication and subsequent diversification give rise to three homologous kinesin I proteins (KIF5A, KIF5B and KIF5C) in vertebrates.
source: Gene duplication and subsequent diversification give rise to three homologous kinesin I proteins (KIF5A, KIF5B and KIF5C) in vertebrates, but it is not clear whether and how they exhibit functional specificity.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as background information

claim: The functional specificities of KIF5A and KIF5B are determined by their diverse carboxyl-termini.
source: The functional specificities of the two kinesins are determined by their diverse carboxyl-termini, where arginine methylation occurs in KIF5B and regulates its function.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding

claim: Arginine methylation occurs in KIF5B and regulates its function.
source: The functional specificities of the two kinesins are determined by their diverse carboxyl-termini, where arginine methylation occurs in KIF5B and regulates its function.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding, supported by data in Figure 5

claim: KIF5B conditional knockout mice exhibit deficits in dendritic spine morphogenesis, synaptic plasticity and memory formation.
source: KIF5B conditional knockout mice exhibit deficits in dendritic spine morphogenesis, synaptic plasticity and memory formation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding, supported by data in Figures 7 and 8

claim: More than 1000 proteins with diverse structures and functions have been identified in the postsynaptic density (PSD).
source: More than 1000 proteins with diverse structures and functions have been identified in the postsynaptic density (PSD) (Bayés et al., 2011), and a tight regulation of their abundance and localization is essential for proper synapse development and plasticity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bayés et al., 2011

claim: The kinesin superfamily contains 45 members in mammal and is sub-divided into 14 different families based on structural similarity.
source: The kinesin superfamily is very diverse and contains 45 members in mammal. It is sub-divided into 14 different families based on structural similarity (Hirokawa et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirokawa et al., 2010

claim: While only one single KIF5 is present in invertebrates such as Drosophila, C. elegans and Aplysia, gene duplication events give rise to three homologous KIF5 genes (Kif5a, Kif5b and Kif5c) in vertebrates.
source: While only one single KIF5 is present in invertebrates such as Drosophila, C. elegans and Aplysia, gene duplication events give rise to three homologous KIF5 genes (Kif5a, Kif5b and Kif5c) in vertebrates (Miki et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miki et al., 2001

claim: Unlike KIF5B which is ubiquitously expressed, KIF5A and KIF5C are mostly expressed in neuron.
source: Unlike KIF5B which is ubiquitously expressed, KIF5A and KIF5C are mostly expressed in neuron (Kanai et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanai et al., 2000

claim: Functional redundancy has been demonstrated among the three KIF5s, as exogenous expression of KIF5A or KIF5C can rescue the impaired mitochondrial transport in cells lacking KIF5B.
source: Functional redundancy has been demonstrated among the three KIF5s, as exogenous expression of KIF5A or KIF5C can rescue the impaired mitochondrial transport in cells lacking KIF5B (Kanai et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanai et al., 2000

claim: In zebrafish, axonal transport of mitochondria depends only on KIF5A but not the other two KIF5s.
source: In contrast, specific function of individual KIF5 has been reported in zebrafish, in which axonal transport of mitochondria depends only on KIF5A but not the other two KIF5s (Campbell et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campbell et al., 2014

claim: Only KIF5A dysfunction leads to seizure and the neuromuscular disorder Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia.
source: Furthermore, only KIF5A dysfunction leads to seizure and the neuromuscular disorder Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia (Fink, 2013; Nakajima et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fink, 2013 and Nakajima et al., 2012

claim: The three KIF5s contain motor, stalk, and tail domains.
source: The three KIF5s contain motor, stalk, and tail domains (Friedman and Vale, 1999), and they all bind to kinesin light chain (KLC) which mediates interaction with some of the cargoes (Kamal et al., 2000; Morfini et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friedman and Vale, 1999; Kamal et al., 2000; Morfini et al., 2016

claim: All three KIF5s bind to kinesin light chain (KLC) which mediates interaction with some of the cargoes.
source: The three KIF5s contain motor, stalk, and tail domains (Friedman and Vale, 1999), and they all bind to kinesin light chain (KLC) which mediates interaction with some of the cargoes (Kamal et al., 2000; Morfini et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kamal et al., 2000; Morfini et al., 2016

claim: The motor domain of KIF5 preferentially moves out of dendrites into axons.
source: Previous studies have mostly focused on KIF5 function in axonal transport because the motor domain of KIF5 preferentially moves out of dendrites into axons, and KIF5 function is negatively regulated by the dendritic protein MAP2 (Gumy et al., 2017; Huang and Banker, 2012; Kapitein et al., 2010; Tas et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gumy et al., 2017; Huang and Banker, 2012; Kapitein et al., 2010; Tas et al., 2017

claim: KIF5 function is negatively regulated by the dendritic protein MAP2.
source: Previous studies have mostly focused on KIF5 function in axonal transport because the motor domain of KIF5 preferentially moves out of dendrites into axons, and KIF5 function is negatively regulated by the dendritic protein MAP2 (Gumy et al., 2017; Huang and Banker, 2012; Kapitein et al., 2010; Tas et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gumy et al., 2017; Huang and Banker, 2012; Kapitein et al., 2010; Tas et al., 2017

claim: All three KIF5s are co-purified with RNPs.
source: However, all three KIF5s are co-purified with RNPs, and dominant-negative KIF5 disrupts the dendritic localization of RNA-binding proteins (Kanai et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanai et al., 2004

claim: Dominant-negative KIF5 disrupts the dendritic localization of RNA-binding proteins.
source: However, all three KIF5s are co-purified with RNPs, and dominant-negative KIF5 disrupts the dendritic localization of RNA-binding proteins (Kanai et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanai et al., 2004

claim: Dendritic cargoes for KIF5 include the AMPA receptor/GRIP1 complex and GABAA receptor.
source: Additional dendritic cargoes for KIF5, including the AMPA receptor/GRIP1 complex and GABAA receptor, have also been identified (Heisler et al., 2014; Nakajima et al., 2012; Setou et al., 2002; Twelvetrees et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heisler et al., 2014; Nakajima et al., 2012; Setou et al., 2002; Twelvetrees et al., 2010

claim: Mushroom spines are regarded as mature spines that are more stable and possess the excitatory PSD.
source: We focus on mushroom spines instead of the other three spine types in subsequent experiments because mushroom spines are regarded as mature spines that are more stable and possess the excitatory PSD (Bourne and Harris, 2007; Berry and Nedivi, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bourne and Harris, 2007; Berry and Nedivi, 2017

claim: Depletion of FMRP in mouse brain resulted in an increase of dendritic filopodia.
source: This may explain the altered spine morphology after knockdown of KIF5B, since the depletion of FMRP in mouse brain also resulted in an increase of dendritic filopodia (Comery et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Comery et al., 1997

claim: The local translation of CaMKIIα and Grin2b mRNAs is critical to synaptic plasticity.
source: The local translation of CaMKIIα and Grin2b mRNAs is critical to synaptic plasticity (Kuklin et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2007), which may contribute to the disrupted LTP in mouse hippocampus upon KIF5B depletion.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuklin et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2007

claim: FMRP and associated mRNA transport involves interaction with KLC.
source: FMRP and associated mRNA transport involves interaction with KLC (Dictenberg et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dictenberg et al., 2008

claim: Different KIFs transport cargoes with different velocities.
source: It was recently reported that different KIFs transport cargoes with different velocities and MAP2 inhibits KIF5B activity in dendrites by interacting with the coiled-coil region and blocking microtubule binding (Gumy et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gumy et al., 2017

claim: MAP2 inhibits KIF5B activity in dendrites by interacting with the coiled-coil region and blocking microtubule binding.
source: It was recently reported that different KIFs transport cargoes with different velocities and MAP2 inhibits KIF5B activity in dendrites by interacting with the coiled-coil region and blocking microtubule binding (Gumy et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gumy et al., 2017

claim: Microtubule and dynein are required for mRNA anchoring in Drosophila embryos.
source: Alternatively, since microtubule and dynein are required for mRNA anchoring in Drosophila embryos (Delanoue and Davis, 2005), it is possible that besides a conventional transport function, KIF5s may help anchoring the dendritically localized FMRP and mRNAs near synapses for local translation in response to extracellular stimuli such as BDNF or synaptic activity (Schratt, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delanoue and Davis, 2005; Schratt, 2004

claim: CaMKII-mediated phosphorylation of KIF17 disrupts the interaction with the adaptor protein LIN10 and unloads the NMDA receptor subunit 2B (GluN2B) containing vesicles.
source: Previous studies on the Kinesin-2 motor protein KIF17 revealed a novel mechanism of cargo release through calmodulin-dependent protein kinase (CaMKII)-mediated phosphorylation, which disrupts the interaction with the adaptor protein LIN10 and unloads the NMDA receptor subunit 2B (GluN2B) containing vesicles (Guillaud et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guillaud et al., 2008

claim: The association between synaptotagmin-containing vesicles and the motor adaptor UNC76 of KIF5 in Drosophila is strengthened by phosphorylation.
source: On the other hand, the association between synaptotagmin-containing vesicles and the motor adaptor UNC76 of KIF5 in Drosophila is strengthened by phosphorylation (Toda et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Toda et al., 2008

claim: Increase in dendritic spine instability has been commonly found in various disease models, such as Fragile X syndrome, schizophrenia, spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 and Huntington disease.
source: Increase in dendritic spine instability has been commonly found in various disease models, such as Fragile X syndrome (Nagaoka et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2010), schizophrenia (Fénelon et al., 2013), spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (Hatanaka et al., 2015) and Huntington disease (Murmu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nagaoka et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2010; Fénelon et al., 2013; Hatanaka et al., 2015; Murmu et al., 2013

claim: A small fraction of the population of transient spines that grows after experience or behavioral training over days can be stabilized over the animal's lifetime, contributing to long-lasting circuit remodeling associated with new experience.
source: It has been found that a small fraction of the population of transient spines grows after experience or behavioral training over days can be stabilized over the animal's lifetime, contributing to long-lasting circuit remodeling associated with new experience (Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2009

claim: The synaptic tagging and capture hypothesis proposes that the synapses activated during LTP induction become 'tagged'.
source: The synaptic tagging and capture hypothesis proposes that the synapses activated during LTP induction become 'tagged' (Rogerson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rogerson et al., 2014

claim: The reduction of mEPSC frequency in the GFP-positive neuron was likely due to cell-autonomous decrease in synapse number on the postsynaptic neuron instead of change in presynaptic release.
source: Since the shRNA and GFP constructs were introduced to the neurons using calcium phosphate precipitation which has very low transfection efficiency, the reduction of mEPSC frequency in the GFP-positive neuron was likely due to cell-autonomous decrease in synapse number on the postsynaptic neuron instead of change in presynaptic release.
evidence: Inferred from the low transfection efficiency of calcium phosphate precipitation method

claim: KIF5A and KIF5B have intrinsically distinct functions on excitatory synapses.
source: These findings indicate that KIF5A and KIF5B have intrinsically distinct functions on excitatory synapses, although both KIF5A and KIF5B can be found in dendritic spines.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing differential effects of KIF5A and KIF5B

claim: A subset of proteins and/or mRNAs may depend on KIF5B for the delivery to mushroom spines that confer their selective maintenance.
source: At the molecular level, we have also identified the postsynaptic scaffolding protein STRN4, which is encoded by a dendritic mRNA and its expression depends on NMDA receptor activity, is involved specifically in the maintenance of mushroom spines (Lin et al., 2017). It is tempting to speculate that a subset of proteins and/or mRNAs may depend on KIF5B for the delivery to mushroom spines that confer their selective maintenance.
evidence: Speculative statement based on previous findings about STRN4

claim: Different pools of FMRP granules are carried by different KIFs, with KIF5B mainly responsible for the less motile granules while other KIFs transport the more motile pools of FMRP.
source: Since other kinesins besides KIF5 can also bind to FMRP (Charalambous et al., 2013; Davidovic et al., 2007), we speculate that different pools of FMRP granules are carried by different KIFs, with KIF5B mainly responsible for the less motile granules while other KIFs transport the more motile pools of FMRP.
evidence: Speculative statement based on differential effects on granule motility and cited literature

claim: The impaired synaptic function due to KIF5B deficiency cannot be compensated by KIF5C in the postnatal brain.
source: However, in the KIF5B conditional knockout mice in which KIF5C expression remains unaffected, reduction in both spine density and mEPSC is observed in hippocampal neurons. Therefore, the impaired synaptic function due to KIF5B deficiency cannot be compensated by KIF5C in the postnatal brain.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that KIF5C cannot rescue deficits in KIF5B knockout mice

claim: KIF5B is the more prominently expressed kinesin compared to KIF5C in the adult hippocampus.
source: One possible explanation is that KIF5B is the more prominently expressed kinesin compared to KIF5C in the adult hippocampus as shown by quantitative immunoblot (Kanai et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanai et al., 2000

claim: The carboxyl terminus may not bind to cargo directly since GST-KIF5B constructs without this region still pull down various cargoes.
source: The carboxyl terminus may not bind to cargo directly since GST-KIF5B constructs without this region (a.a. 936–963) still pull down various cargoes (Setou et al., 2002; Cho et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2010; Barry et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from cited studies showing cargo binding without carboxyl terminus

claim: The longer carboxyl-terminus of KIF5A binds directly to GABAA receptor-associated protein for the development of inhibitory synapses.
source: In this regard, it is noteworthy that the longer carboxyl-terminus of KIF5A binds directly to GABAA receptor-associated protein for the development of inhibitory synapses (Nakajima et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakajima et al., 2012

claim: There is a division of labor among the two KIF5s in regulating excitatory and inhibitory synapses, and the evolution of their diverse carboxyl-termini confer them functional specificities.
source: Our findings together raise the interesting possibility that there is a division of labor among the two KIF5s in regulating excitatory and inhibitory synapses, and the evolution of their diverse carboxyl-termini confer them functional specificities.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the findings about differential functions of KIF5A and KIF5B

claim: Many axonal cargoes, such as syntabulin, SNAP25 and amyloid precursor protein (APP) have been identified for KIF5s.
source: Many axonal cargoes, such as syntabulin, SNAP25 and amyloid precursor protein (APP) have been identified for KIF5s (Hirokawa and Tanaka, 2015; Kamal et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hirokawa and Tanaka, 2015; Kamal et al., 2000

claim: KIF5 motor domain predominately recognizes axonal rather than dendritic microtubules.
source: KIF5 motor domain also predominately recognizes axonal rather than dendritic microtubules, which highlight its functional significance in axon (Kapitein et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kapitein et al., 2010

claim: KIF5B is localized not only in the axons, but is also present in the dendrites and dendritic spines of dissociated hippocampal neurons.
source: We found that KIF5B is localized not only in the axons, but is also present in the dendrites and dendritic spines of dissociated hippocampal neurons, supporting the role of dendritic KIF5B in the development of excitatory postsynaptic sites.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Microtubule invasion to the spine heads from dendritic shaft is crucial for dendritic spine plasticity.
source: Although it was originally thought that microtubule is not present in dendritic spines, emerging study has revealed the invasion of microtubule and kinesin to the spine heads from dendritic shaft, which are crucial for dendritic spine plasticity (Jaworski et al., 2009; McVicker et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jaworski et al., 2009; McVicker et al., 2016

claim: KIF5B might represent one of the kinesin motors that deliver synaptic proteins to the dendritic spines.
source: Our findings suggest that KIF5B might represent one of the kinesin motors that deliver synaptic proteins to the dendritic spines.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the localization and function of KIF5B

claim: Different spine types can be regulated differentially and independently.
source: It is interesting that knockdown of KIF5B specifically decreases mushroom spines in cultured hippocampal neurons while increasing the abundance of the other three types of spines. Emerging studies have demonstrated that different spine types can be regulated differentially and independently (Sanders et al., 2012; Spiga et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sanders et al., 2012; Spiga et al., 2014

claim: The lack of dendritic spine density difference in the frontal association cortex between wild-type and KIF5B conditional knockout mice could be due to the delay of frontal cortex maturation and pruning in the conditional knockout mutant.
source: Since the frontal cortex maturation happens at later developmental stage (Caballero et al., 2016; Gogtay et al., 2004; Zuo et al., 2005), the lack of dendritic spine density difference in the frontal association cortex between wild-type and KIF5B conditional knockout mice could be due to the delay of frontal cortex maturation and pruning in the conditional knockout mutant.
evidence: Speculative statement based on developmental timing of frontal cortex maturation

claim: The deficits observed in KIF5B conditional knockout mice could be stemmed from the impairment of PRP trafficking specifically delivered by KIF5B in dendrites in response to activity-dependent plasticity.
source: The deficits that we observed in KIF5B conditional knockout mice could be stemmed from the impairment of PRP trafficking specifically delivered by KIF5B in dendrites in response to activity-dependent plasticity.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the synaptic tagging and capture hypothesis

claim: Homologous members of the other kinesin families may also exhibit functional specificity in the brain.
source: It is plausible that homologous members of the other kinesin families also exhibit functional specificity in the brain, an interesting research area which warrants further study in the future.
evidence: Speculative statement extrapolating from findings about KIF5 family

claim: Conditional knockout of Kif5b causes memory recall deficits in social memory, object recognition memory, fear associative memory, and spatial memory tests, with no significant deficit during initial memory acquisition phase.
source: Here we demonstrated that specific knockout of Kif5b in CaMKIIα-expressing neurons leads to deficits in memory recall in social memory, novel object recognition, auditory-cued fear conditioning, and spatial memory tests, with no significant deficit during initial memory acquisition phase.
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 8

claim: The synaptic and memory deficits in the KIF5B conditional knockout mice cannot be compensated by the presence of the other two homologous KIF5s.
source: Moreover, the synaptic and memory deficits in the KIF5B conditional knockout mice cannot be compensated by the presence of the other two homologous KIF5s.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of deficits despite presence of KIF5A and KIF5C
